summary: Describes use cases for RANGER, an architectural framework for scalable routing and addressing described in RFC 5720. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Examples showing how one proposed plan for organizing internet addresses and routes would work in real situations.

questions: routing and addressing global enterprise recursion
subtitle: Use cases for a map-and-encapsulate architecture to solve routing and addressing problems.

tldr.problem: The Internet faces scaling problems in its core routing tables due to address depletion, multihoming, and traffic engineering demands, and operators need solutions for recursively nested networks, enterprise-to-enterprise connections, and IPv4-to-IPv6 transitions.
tldr.mechanism: RANGER (Routing and Addressing in Networks with Global Enterprise Recursion) provides an architectural framework using a 'map and encapsulate' approach: Enterprise Border Routers form overlay networks by encapsulating traffic across a commons, separating Endpoint Interface iDentifiers (globally unique addresses) from Routing Locators (enterprise-local addresses).
tldr.outcome: The architecture enables scalable, provider-independent, multihomed, and mobile networks at any level of the IP Topology Hierarchy, from small offices to the entire Internet, without requiring changes to most hosts or routers.

facts.label: Recursion limit
facts.value: Enterprise Border Router (EBR) is the limiting factor

today: RFC 6139 is an Informational RFC that remains current as part of the RANGER architecture series. While RANGER itself has not become a mandatory part of the Internet standards, its principles have influenced ongoing work in routing scalability, including locator-identifier separation protocols (LISP) and various provider-independent multihoming approaches. The document continues to serve as a reference for enterprises and service providers seeking architectural frameworks that support scalable, provider-independent, multihomed deployments.

sections.title: The Scaling Challenge
sections.content:
The Internet has grown to become critical infrastructure for business, government, and individuals worldwide. This growth strains core routing systems: IPv4 address space is becoming depleted, Regional Internet Registries have passed the 86% allocation threshold, and multihoming with provider-independent addresses has caused the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) routing table in the Internet's Default-Free Zone to grow far beyond what was originally expected.

RANGER (Routing and Addressing in Networks with Global Enterprise Recursion) carries forward architectural principles from earlier designs like NIMROD and the Catenet model, reimagining how networks can be organized. Rather than a flat hierarchy, RANGER introduces recursive 'enterprise-within-enterprise' structures that allow networks to be nested at any level, from a single router up to the entire Internet. This recursion enables each network to maintain its own independent internal addressing and routing, reducing the burden on the global core.
sections.eli5: The internet's address books and route maps are getting too big and complicated. A new design lets networks be built inside other networks, like boxes within boxes, so each layer doesn't have to track everything globally.

sections.title: Core Architectural Elements
sections.content:
RANGER's key innovation is the separation of two address spaces: Endpoint Interface iDentifiers (EIDs), which are globally unique addresses assigned to end systems and edge network interfaces, and Routing Locators (RLOCs), which are locally significant addresses used within each enterprise network's interior routing. An enterprise can use any address space for its RLOCs (including overlapping private space), because routing within the enterprise is isolated.

Enterprise Border Routers (EBRs) sit at the edges of enterprise networks and tunnel traffic across shared infrastructure called a 'commons' (such as the global Internet or an ISP network). When an EBR needs to reach a destination EID, it consults a mapping system (similar to DNS or BGP) to find the RLOC address of the remote EBR that can reach that EID. It then encapsulates the packet using IP-in-IP tunneling and sends it across the commons. The receiving EBR decapsulates the packet and forwards it normally to the destination. This approach means the routing tables in the commons only need to know about RLOCs and EBRs, not every EID, which dramatically reduces routing state.
sections.eli5: RANGER uses two kinds of addresses: ones for your immediate network (RLOCs) and ones that work everywhere (EIDs). Special routers at network boundaries use a lookup table to tunnel packets between networks, so the main internet only has to track the border routers, not all the computers inside.

sections.title: Global and Enterprise Scenarios
sections.content:
For the global Internet, RANGER addresses scaling by allowing autonomous systems to function as enterprise networks with their own independent RLOC spaces, while using larger EID prefixes (such as IPv6) for global endpoints. This separates the growth in endpoint addresses from the growth in core routing state.

For large corporate enterprises, RANGER enables support of complex structures without renumbering: a merged corporation with two incompatible internal address spaces can continue using both by designating their internal networks as separate RLOC domains while providing a unified EID address space to end systems. Multihomed enterprises can connect to multiple service providers using provider-independent EID prefixes, which the mapping system advertises to the commons without requiring every router to know about every connection.

Small office networks (SOHO) can use RANGER to grow without readdressing: a small company initially behind a NAT can deploy an EBR alongside its existing firewall, allowing public services (like web servers) to have EID addresses while legacy systems continue using RFC 1918 private RLOCs. As the company expands to multiple locations or moves to new ISPs, the EID-based services remain reachable without renumbering.
sections.eli5: Big networks can use different address styles internally while looking the same on the outside. Small companies can keep their old addresses inside while publishing a new address style for servers. Moving to a new service provider does not require renumbering anything.

sections.title: Transition and IPv4-IPv6 Coexistence
sections.content:
RANGER supports long-term coexistence of IPv4 and IPv6 by allowing each level of the network hierarchy to independently choose its EID and RLOC address families. An enterprise network could use IPv6 internally as RLOCs while providing IPv4 EIDs to legacy applications, or vice versa. The mapping system and tunneling mechanism remain address-family agnostic.

This decoupling allows enterprises and service providers to migrate to IPv6 independently in their core (RLOC space) without requiring all end systems to migrate simultaneously. Applications can continue using IPv4, while the underlying network transitions to IPv6 at the operator's pace. Mobile networks and first-responder systems benefit from RANGER's ability to maintain end-to-end identifiers (EIDs) while moving across different network infrastructure.
sections.eli5: Different parts of the network can use old-style or new-style addresses independently. You can switch the core to new addresses while keeping old address style for applications, or any combination.

sections.title: Relationship to Other Approaches
sections.content:
RANGER builds on earlier architectural work including the ROAD group deliberations, NIMROD, and the Catenet model. It incorporates functional components from Virtual Enterprise Traversal (VET) for tunneling, Subnetwork Encapsulation and Adaptation Layer (SEAL) for robust packet handling, and ISATAP for automatic tunneling. The RFC shows how RANGER principles apply from a single router scale up to the entire Internet, making it a general-purpose framework.

The document expands on concepts from earlier RFC 4057 (IPv6 Enterprise Network Scenarios) and RFC 4852 (IPv6 Enterprise Network Analysis). Unlike some competing approaches that assume specific protocols or address families, RANGER is compatible with multiple standards work ongoing in the IETF, including LISP (Locator/ID Separation Protocol), APT (A Practical Transit Mapping Service), and FIB suppression with virtual aggregation.
sections.eli5: RANGER takes ideas from much older network designs and mixes them with modern tunneling and mapping technology to create a system that works at every scale.

sections.title: Application Examples and Next Steps
sections.content:
The RFC presents detailed scenarios showing RANGER in action. A single Enterprise Border Router can be viewed as an enterprise itself, enabling recursion down to the granularity of individual hosts. Large corporations with multiple locations and ISP connections can support independent internal addressing while presenting a unified EID-based face to the Internet. Service providers can use RANGER to support cellular networks, aeronautical networks, and unmanaged wireless networks. The mapping and encapsulation machinery enables secure connections across untrusted infrastructure and restoration of end-to-end transparency originally envisioned for the Internet.

The document serves as a use-case catalog inviting criticism, comments, and exploration of whether RANGER principles can help guide the next-generation Internet architecture. By showing how the framework addresses diverse requirements—scalability, mobility, multihoming, security, and IPv4-IPv6 transition—it demonstrates that the same architectural principles apply across networks of any size or purpose.
sections.eli5: This RFC gives many examples of how RANGER could be used: small companies growing, big corporations merging, mobile networks, airplane networks, and others. It shows that the same design works for all of them.
